Custom LLM metrics for AI agent evaluation

Our metrics could prove an agent called the right tool, not that its answer was any good. I designed a no-code way for builders to turn their own criteria into an LLM judge, and test it before it scores anything that matters.

Where it landed

Describe what good looks like, get a complete judge, test it on something that really happened, and only then publish it.

  • No scriptingPlain-language answers generate the complete judge prompt, rubric included.
  • Tested before trustedPublish stays locked until a test is on record. Edit the prompt and it locks again.
  • Fits the pipelineCustom scores use the same result shape as built-in metrics, so they sit side by side.

The problem

Our metrics graded the process, not the outcome

They could confirm an agent chose and called the right tool. Customers wanted to know whether the answer was right.

01Discover

Ten people who evaluate agents for a living

UX research interviewed six quality engineers and four managers, an hour each. They build the agents customers get out of the box: if our metrics failed them, they would fail customers too.

Quality engineer Manager 60-minute semi-structured interviews
7 business units, including HRSDITSMSPMSecOpsCRMPlatform

Five reasons teams stopped using the built-in metrics

Binary scoring

A right-or-wrong result won't get a feature approved. Teams rebuilt the same metric on a 1–5 rubric.

“If you tell me it is sixty percent good, I'll be more confident to push the feature out.”

Process, not outcome

Metrics checked whether the agent called the right tool. Customers ask what it achieved.

“All they want is output eval.”

No sense of context

One definition of completeness can't serve summarisation, security analysis and an HR workflow at once.

Graceful failures score as wins

A workflow that exits through its own error path still counts as a completed task.

“The agent has taken a failure route but I see that the metric says success”

Scores that flatter

Results landed above 90% while manual review said the experience was worse.

The maturity model that reframed the ask

Teams sat at three levels, and each needed something different from us. The design had to serve all three.

Level 1 Foundational

Uses built-in metrics as they are, often unaware customising is possible.

Needs from usTo know a better fit exists

A library that shows what already exists

Level 2 Developing

Clones a built-in and rewrites the judge prompt for one use case. Rarely reuses it.

Needs from usA supported clone-and-edit path

Start from a template, edit it safely

Level 3 Advanced

Runs on outcome-based custom metrics; keeps built-ins for debugging steps.

Needs from usA library, versions and consistent scoring

Versions, and judges tested before publishing

02Define

A domain expert, not a prompt engineer

The person who knows what a good resolution note looks like is rarely the person who enjoys writing an evaluation script.

Sam

AI practitioner

Technical enough to build an agent, and specific enough to know exactly where it falls short.

  • Builds and tests both the agent and the metric
  • Works inside the customer's company, enabling its employees or customers

Needs

  • Judge quality on business-specific criteria
  • Create a metric without writing a script
  • Test a metric before publishing it
  • See why a score came out the way it did
  • Reuse and share metrics instead of rebuilding

Pain points

  • One built-in definition can't capture the nuance
  • The only workaround is too technical
  • No way to know whether to trust a score
  • Hard to find; the workflow is split across surfaces
  • No guidance on how to create a metric

Sam's path to a custom metric, today

The research findings laid out as a journey. Each low point lines up with the part of the design that answers it.

Swipe sideways to see the whole journey

What the session settled. An evaluation result has to answer three things: what went wrong, where, and how to fix it. That branch of the map became the testing system.

A prompt box is easy. A judge a team will ship on is not.

Four things decide whether anyone trusts an LLM judge. Each one got a mechanism in the product, not a warning in the docs.

Non-determinism

Same input, three runs

Run 10.90
Run 20.20
Run 30.85

A judge that returns 0.9, then 0.2, then 0.85 on comparable input is worth nothing.

Temperature 0.1 by default, a fixed output format, and results that pile up so the spread is visible before publishing.

Rubric drift

No fixed rubric, three runs

Run 14 / 5
Run 27 / 10
Run 3Pass?

Without a fixed rubric the model invents a new scale every run, so scores stop being comparable.

The rubric is captured at creation. Dimensions and scale belong to the metric, not the model.

Input-mapping fragility

The judge's context

Resolution note: {{resolution_note}}

0.0No error shown

If test inputs don't map to the prompt's variables, the judge scores half the context and fails silently.

Variables come from the execution context. Each becomes its own labelled test field, never one free-text box.

The language gap

“A good note says what happened.”

?

Action takenRoot causeNext steps

Builders describe quality in domain terms. Judges need evaluator-precise criteria. Reliability is won or lost in between.

Guided questions turn plain-language anchors into structured criteria, and a quality signal flags gaps before testing.

Nothing publishes untestedStart complete, never blankShow variance, never average it awayEvery score carries its reason
Nothing publishes untestedStart complete, never blankShow variance, never average it awayEvery score carries its reason

Six rules the design enforces

Each closes a failure we watched happen, and each costs the user a little freedom on purpose.

  • Start complete, never blankThe full judge prompt, rubric included, is generated before the editor opens.
  • Ask in a fixed orderAgent scope first, because it decides which context variables exist.
  • Lock what scoring depends onRole, output format and guardrails stay system-owned: visible, never breakable.
  • Nothing publishes untestedPublish unlocks after a recorded test. Edit the prompt and it locks again.
  • Show variance, never average it awayEvery test adds a row. No cross-run average hides the spread.
  • Every score carries its reasonA plain-language justification ships with every score. A failed call is an error, not a zero.

04Design

Three systems, each only as good as the one before it

A weak answer early becomes a wrong score later, so two checkpoints sit between the systems.

  1. System 1Input elicitation
  3. System 2Generation and refinement
  4. Prompt quality signal
  5. System 3Testing and trust
  6. Publish gate
  7. FoundationLibrary, versions and one result contract
System 1Input elicitation

Ask for judgement, not prompt craft

Three short steps, in a fixed order, in a modal over the library.

1

Scope and intent first

Agent scope decides which context variables exist. The description shapes the judge most, so it is asked plainly and early.

2

Start from a proven pattern

Templates come from judges that already existed but were never surfaced here. The prompt is previewable before it is added.

3

Choose the shape of the answer

Scoring type, categories and a good and a poor example are captured before anything is generated, so rubric, schema and aggregation agree.

Every answer has a home in the prompt

This is the translation a domain expert shouldn't have to do by hand. Select an answer to see where it lands.

Three shapes of answer, chosen before anything is generated

The choice sets the rubric, the aggregation and the output schema, so it can't come after.

Teams dropped the built-ins partly because a binary result wouldn't get a feature approved. The shape of the answer is why they'll use the metric at all.

The one wait in the flow. What arrives is a complete judge, which is the point of asking structured questions first.

System 2Generation and refinement

Start complete, then refine safely

The judge arrives finished. Editing it is reversible, and the parts scoring depends on are locked.

1

Progress you can count

Steps to publish states what's done and what's left, and links to it, so the gate teaches instead of blocking.

2

Edit with assistance, reversibly

Select a passage, refine it with AI, then append or replace, with undo always there. The pattern is borrowed from another team.

System 3Testing and trust

Earn trust by watching it judge something real

Pick a real execution, read the score and its reason, give your own score, and see how often you agree.

1

Test on something that happened

Pick a solution, a version and an actual execution. Each prompt variable gets its own labelled input.

2

Score, output and setup in one view

The prompt stays beside the result, so diagnosing a strange score never loses your place.

3

The justification is the product

A number says look. The justification says where. Then you give your own score.

4

Calibration you can actually run

You score, the judge scores, and the panel reports how often you agree. A lightweight trust check that needs no labelled dataset.

FoundationLibrary and versions

A library that remembers which criteria made which score

Published metrics are versioned and pre-selected for the agent they were built for.

{ score, justification, status }the same result shape as every built-in metric, so a custom score renders next to task completeness with no special casing

On a phoneThe same flow, every screen

Five rules decided how every screen fits a phone

Fifteen phone screens, grouped by the rule that shaped them.

  1. Tables become cards Rows turn into cards that keep what people scan for.

  2. LibraryEach row keeps status, scope and provider

  3. Modals become full-screen steps A progress bar replaces the step title. Back and Continue stay at the bottom.

  4. DefineProgress on top, actions at the bottom

  5. TemplateOptional, so Skip is the main action

  6. ScoringStill chosen before anything is generated

  7. CreatingThe one wait, full screen

  8. The section rail becomes tabs Save, Run test and Publish move into a bar at the bottom.

  9. Metric promptSections become tabs; actions dock below

  10. ProcessorsOne section per tab

  11. Model settingsSave, Run test and Publish stay in reach

  12. Popovers and side panels become bottom sheets Each one opens over the page it belongs to.

  13. Steps to publishThe sheet names the next step

  14. Prompt editThe passage being refined stays in view

  15. Version detailsPlaceholders say what to write

  16. Run testSearch runs, or tap a recent one

  17. Side by side becomes its own page The one trade-off: prompt and result no longer share a screen. The test is one tap back.

  18. Test resultThe test gets a page of its own

  19. Setup detailsTabs replace side-by-side panels

  20. Score comparisonIts table becomes cards too

The definition of good changes

Editing a published metric creates a new version, and every run records the version it used.

05Deliver

Build the smallest loop that works, then earn the right to add

First prove one builder can define, test and reuse one business-specific judge. Everything after that is sequenced, not rejected.

MVPDefine a metric in plain language, no scripting

Input-based creation, a generated judge prompt, single-test calibration, the library and versions.

NextValidate at scale against real datasets

DataKit integration, bulk testing and dataset-based calibration.

ThenScore complex, multi-part criteria

Multi-criteria metrics, weighted scoring, building a metric conversationally.

HorizonOptimise judges automatically

Trace-based context and automated prompt optimisation, once labelled data exists.

In the MVP, and deliberately not yet

AreaIn the MVPNot yetWhy
AuthoringStructured inputsConversational creationReliability over ambiguity
ValidationSingle-test calibrationBulk judge-the-judge, annotationsAvoid a dataset dependency
ContextExecution parser variablesTools framework, trace dependencyAvoid a platform blocker
OptimisationMetric quality signalsAutomated prompt optimisationNeeds labelled datasets
ComplexitySingle criterionMulti-criteria, multi-judgeProve the baseline first

A version already shipped, and almost nobody uses it

Custom LLM metrics already exist inside the Skill Kit evaluation experience. Three months of telemetry, June to August 2026, is the number this work has to move.

How we'll know it worked

Usability

A builder defines a business-specific metric without scripting or prompt engineering.

Measured by input completion, and how many who start a metric publish one
Trust

A builder tests judge behaviour before publishing or reusing it.

Measured by every published metric having a recorded test. The gate works, or it's a defect.
Operational fit

The metric runs inside AutoEval and maps to the same result contract as everything else.

Measured by run completion and telemetry coverage

Instrumented at launch

  • Tests run before a metric is published: how much iteration trust actually takes
  • New or reused custom metric at run setup: whether the library does its job
  • Justifications expanded: whether people engage past the number
  • Runs completed with at least one custom metric: the primary adoption signal

Where the risk still sits

  • Judge inconsistency could undermine trust early. A real variance baseline still needs an engineering spike.
  • Reliability depends on input quality, which can't be validated automatically.
  • Generation runs on a small model today; a complete, context-aware judge may need a larger one.
  • Context is built on today's parser. Moving to traces later is a real migration.

The numeric targets behind these signals are product proposals, not engineering commitments: a starting point for kickoff, and saying so is part of the work.

Reflection

What I'd carry into the next one

  • Trust is a design material.The gate, the variance rows and the justifications do more for confidence than any explanation could.
  • Structure is kinder than a blank box.A domain expert can refine a strong draft. Nobody should have to author a judge from nothing.
  • Say “not yet”, with a reason.Sequencing the bigger ideas, instead of rejecting them, kept the MVP small without losing the roadmap.

A team should be able to say what good looks like for their agent in their own words, watch a judge apply it to something that really happened, disagree with it, and only then let it score anyone else's work.

That sentence is the test every screen here had to pass.
